covers.quote: Use initial capitals for:
the official name of a country
any commonly used short forms of the country’s name
the names of states, territories and provinces.
The definite article ‘the’ isn’t capitalised unless it begins a sentence.

examples.note: Initial capitals on country and shortened forms, with lowercase 'the'.
Initial capitals on country and shortened forms, with lowercase 'the'.

rules.quote: Spell country names with a capital letter
rules.violation_condition: a country name, commonly used short form, or state/territory/province name written without an initial capital letter, or the definite article 'the' capitalised before a country name mid-sentence
when: The definite article 'the' is not capitalised unless it begins a sentence.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: The heading states the rule; list items elaborate which entities take initial capitals, and the exception for 'the' is an exception (G-3).

covers.quote: Shorten a country name only if it is clear to the user

parts.quote: ‘North Korea’ is the shortened form of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea.

rules.quote: Use a short form of a country’s name only if it’s clear and accurate.
rules.violation_condition: a shortened country name used in a context where it is not clear or accurate
rules.why: G-4: The body sentence states the condition clearly; the heading is consolidated.

covers.quote: Use English versions of countries and places in most content
English-language content usually uses the English version of a country’s name.
There are some cases where the preferred official name isn’t in English.

parts.quote: ‘Socialist Republic of Vietnam’ is the English version of Cộng hòa xã hội chủ nghĩa Việt Nam.
‘Germany’ is the English version of Deutschland.

examples.note: Exception where non-English form is preferred official name.

parts.quote: ‘Côte d’Ivoire’ is the preferred official name for the Ivory Coast.

examples.note: Established English form for well-known place name.

rules.quote: In English-speaking countries, the convention is to use the established English forms for well-known place names.
rules.violation_condition: a non-English form used for a well-known place name in general English content where an established English form exists (except where an official non-English name is preferred)
when: In some cases, the preferred official name is not in English (e.g. Côte d’Ivoire, Eswatini).
rules.why: G-2, G-4: The heading and body sentences articulate the general rule and exception to use established English forms.

rules.quote: When the name is used generically, you don’t need an initial capital.
rules.violation_condition: a place name capitalised when used in a generic sense as part of a common item or term
when: Applies when a place name is used generically (e.g. types of items) rather than referring to the place itself.
rules.why: G-2: Specific rule governing capitalisation for genericised geographical names.

covers.quote: Check the official status for area and region names

rules.quote: Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.
rules.violation_condition: a recognized political or geographic group of nations or area written without initial capitals
rules.why: G-4, G-5: The heading is advisory ('Check official status'); the body states the capitalisation requirement.

examples.note: Lowercase compass direction used as modifier.
Lowercase compass direction used as modifier.

rules.quote: Use lower case if the names of compass points (such as north and south-east) are not part of the name but are used to refer to the geographic area.
rules.violation_condition: a compass point capitalised when it is not part of an official name but merely refers to a geographic area
when: Compass point is not an official part of the proper name.
rules.why: G-2: Clear negative instruction on when to lowercase compass points.

covers.quote: Capitalise the names of certain groups.

parts.quote: People groups – Hispanic, Sentinelese, Vietnamese Rục, Sámi
People who follow particular religions – Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Greek Orthodox

rules.quote: Write nationalities, peoples and places with initial capitals
rules.violation_condition: the name of a nationality, people group, clan, regional group, religious group, or language-speaker group written without an initial capital
rules.why: G-4: Heading gives the direct instruction; body sentence restates it for certain groups.
